place.zh: 沉鼎观 · 外门 · 执事房
place.en: Chending Temple · The outer court · the steward's office

setup.zh: 晌午歇场。第十七条：一炷香里交十块灵石，能复试一场。你怀里一块也没有；周衡不先支。
setup.en: The noon break. Rule seventeen: ten spirit stones within one stick of incense buys a second trial. You haven't one; Zhou Heng won't pay in advance.

recap.zh: 你输了第一轮。复试要十块灵石，周衡不先支；你把爷爷的弓当在了钱掌柜那里——子时不赎，弓便姓钱。
recap.en: You lost the first round. The second trial cost ten stones and Zhou Heng wouldn't pay in advance; you pawned your grandfather's bow with Money-Keeper Qian — not redeemed by midnight, the bow is his.

zh: 老槐树底下，那张弓横在秤盘上。
en: The noon break. A stick of incense at the stage's corner.
Under the pagoda tree, the bow lies across the scale pan.
"Not redeemed by midnight, the bow's a Qian."

story.zh:
孙二狗的第二轮，对手是柴房那天夜里的五个人里的一个——秘境里抄着手跟在小满身后、给马小宝报信的那一个，崖上饿了三天，这口气还没出。他上台以后，连架势都懒得摆，只把手往背后一背，冲台下马小宝那边笑了一笑，道：「来吧。」孙二狗闭着眼睛冲上去，那人侧身一让，伸脚一勾，他便扑倒在青石板上，下巴磕出了血。

他爬起来了，又冲上去，又扑倒。那人不急着把他推下台，偏往台心上赶，推倒了，等他爬起来，再推倒。执事坐在台角，只盯着那炷香——香没到，人没下台，规矩上便不叫停。台下起先还笑，喊着「二狗，认输吧」「你娘的护身符不管用啦」；到第五回，笑声便稀了；第六回，那人趁他爬到一半，一脚踩在他手背上，碾了一碾，台下有人「嘶」地抽了一口冷气。马小宝在台下拍手：「好！踩得好！谁叫他跟沈小满好！」

小满站在台下，一句话也没说。他的手在袖子里攥着，攥得指甲掐进了肉里。五扇门后头那一圈光，给这一脚踩得往上一窜，窜到他喉咙口，烫得他眼睛发酸。他只要往台上跨一步——一步，那个人便要在半空里转三个圈。可跨了这一步，全观便都看见了：一个验过修为、名册上写着二层的人，一步跨上台，一掌打飞了一个三层的老弟子。胸口的木牌凉凉的，一个很困的声音，只说了一个字：「藏。」

他没有跨。第七回，孙二狗扶着膝盖站起来，满脸是血，腰里那个蓝布包的绳子断了一根，吊在胯骨边上晃荡。他伸手把它捞起来，塞回腰带里，又冲着那人走了过去——不是冲，是走，一步一步，腿抖得跟筛糠一样，每一步都踩得实实在在。那半炷香到了头，执事敲响了铜锣：「停。孙二狗，你还能打么？」孙二狗吐出一口血沫子：「……能。」执事道：「我看不能了。」孙二狗想了想，点点头：「……那就不能了。」他冲执事鞠了一躬，冲那人也鞠了一躬，自己走下了台子。

他没让人扶，一直走到演武场边上那几级石阶跟前，一屁股坐了下去，坐下去便再也站不起来了。小满走过去，在他面前站了一会儿，伸出手去：「起来。地上凉。」孙二狗抓住他的手，他一使劲，把他拉了起来。孙二狗比他高半个头，瘦得一把骨头，拉起来的时候，轻飘飘的，像拉起一根竹竿。九月初九那天，石阶的一百四十级上，有一个兖州来的孩子坐着起不来，小满从他身边走了过去，没有停。他那时想，等我站得够稳了，我要拉。今天他也不算站得多稳，可好歹拉了一个。

那一上午，五行台上打了三轮，三十二个人打剩了四个。内门排头的祁长松，八层，在内门站了二十年桩，上台三回，一步没挪——他往台心那道拼缝上一站，两只脚像钉进了石头，对手打他，打不动，推他，推不动，半炷香一灭，执事一看，台心上站着的是他。内门里管他叫「祁不动」。秦雁上台三回，剑都没出鞘，拿剑鞘一点一拨，三个对手便自己走下了台。马小宝前两回，镜子挂在腰里没摘，一拳一个，拳头砸在青石板上，留下两个白印子。一夜两层的力气，是真的。

第三轮，马小宝对鲁泥鳅。鲁泥鳅上台前，从小满身边挤过去，压低了嗓子：「那面镜子，是我爹的船从下邳捎上来的——马三老爷雇的是我爹的船——在我爹船舱里搁了一路。红布底下，半夜里自己亮过一回——冷的，像泗水底下的光。我爹说，那不是照妖的，是认东西的。」说完，他搓了搓手，上台去了。鲁泥鳅是渔户的儿子，水性好，身子滑，头一拳便钻到了马小宝腋下。马小宝这才摘下了铜镜。

小满站在台下，看得清清楚楚：那面镜子，不是一举就亮的。马小宝两手捧着它，脸上的斑「腾」地一红，一片一片鼓起来，像是有人往他身子里抽东西，抽出来，灌进镜子里——镜面这才亮了，一道黄光扑在鲁泥鳅脸上。鲁泥鳅「哎哟」一声，捂着眼睛倒退，嘴里直叫：「冷的！那光是冷的，往心口钻！」他退一步，马小宝又照一回，斑又红一回，喘得两个肩膀一耸一耸；照到第三回，鲁泥鳅一脚踩空，跌下了台。马小宝捧着镜子，站在那里喘了好一会儿，才喘匀。他冲台下的小满扬了扬下巴。

晌午歇场。周衡站到五行台上，翻开那本蓝布面的名录，清了清嗓子，照着念道：「大比规矩，第十七条：外门弟子输了第一轮的，可纳灵石十块，复试一场。复试者，挑当届外门名册上排头一人；胜，顶他的签，被挑者出局；负，逐下台，灵石不退。」念完了，他从怀里摸出一根香，插在台角的香炉里，点着了，「歇场一炷香。要复试的，香烧完之前，灵石交到执事房。」他又补了一句：「这一条，设了三十年，一回都没人用过。」

台下静了一静，跟着便嗡的一声，一齐转过头来看小满。马小宝的声音从人堆里拔了出来：「他？他拿什么交？他连一块灵石都掏不出来！」一片哄笑。小满站在那里，脸上火辣辣的。他怀里一块灵石也没有；有过的，交了公中，喂了饭桶。

他还是去了执事房。周衡坐在桌后，桌上点着半根蜡烛——他的蜡烛向来只点半根，另外半根掰下来收在抽屉里。小满说：「周师兄，我想复试。」周衡道：「十块。」小满说：「我没有。巡夜簿上那一笔『另议』……能不能先议？」周衡看了他一眼，低下头去翻账簿：「腊八结账，结在晚上。外门的账，没有先支这一说。规矩是规矩。」

小满站了一会儿，出了门。马小宝正倚在执事房门口，手里掂着一块灵石，掂一下，看他一眼，见他出来，把那块灵石往他脚跟前一扔：「捡呀。一块。还差九块。」旁边几个跟班哄地笑了。那块灵石在泥地里滚了两滚，停在小满的草鞋尖上。小满低头看了它一眼，抬脚从它旁边迈了过去。马小宝在他身后道：「沈小满，今年的丹，姓马。」台角那炷香，烧下去一半了。石阶上，孙二狗下巴上贴着伙房大娘给的膏药，贴歪了，他冲小满咧了咧嘴，嘴里还有血。老槐树底下，钱掌柜正拿炭条把「沈小满」后头的「一赔一百」划了，要往上改，想了想，又把炭条放下了——一个输了第一轮、又交不起十块灵石的人，赔率没法往上写了，写多少都是零。

阿禾比他先到了槐树底下。她把那张折成一小块的纸条拍在秤盘上：「掌柜的，我押的那一文，退给我。」钱掌柜抬起眼皮：「押了就是押了。板上写的，就是我说的——押出去的，不退。」阿禾道：「我拿它有急用。」钱掌柜道：「急用也不退。今天给你退了，明天人人来退，我这块板子，就不干净了。」阿禾咬着嘴唇，站了一会儿，没再说话。

阿禾回过头来，看见了小满。她什么也没说，把纸条收回本子里，从他身边走了过去。小满知道她要那一文做什么：一文钱，离十块灵石，差着十万八千里；可她身上，只有那一文。

小满在老槐树底下站住了。他袖子里有一个小瓷瓶，伙房扔的那只辣椒油瓶子，他自己在井边洗了七遍，瓶里一颗丹，十月里饭桶那一地破烂底下滚出来的那一颗回春丹，九道金纹。那是留给他爹的膝盖的——十月里断着肋骨巡夜的那半个月，他都没舍得吃它。这一颗拿到钱掌柜的秤盘上，莫说十块灵石，一百块也换得来。可一颗九道金纹的丹，外门没有一个人见过；拿出去，头一个问的便是「哪来的」——这一问，他答不上来；答不上来，便要搜身、搜柴房，饭桶便藏不住了，银月也藏不住了。何况这是爹的。他攥着那个瓶子，攥得瓶身都热了，到底没有掏出来。
story.en:
Sun Ergou's second round was against one of the five from the woodshed night — the one who'd trailed Xiaoman with folded arms in the hidden realm and run to tell Ma Xiaobao, starved three days on the cliff, the grudge still in him. On the stage he didn't even take a stance; he put his hands behind his back, smiled toward Ma Xiaobao below, and said: "Come on." Sun Ergou charged with his eyes shut; the man stepped aside and hooked a foot, and Sun Ergou went flat on the bluestone and split his chin.

He got up, charged again, fell again. The man wasn't in a hurry to push him off; he herded him toward the centre, knocked him down, waited for him to get up, knocked him down again. The steward sat at the corner of the stage with his eyes on the incense — until it burned down or someone left the stage, the rules said nothing to stop. At first the crowd laughed and shouted, "Ergou, give up!" "Your ma's charm's no good!"; by the fifth time the laughter thinned; the sixth time, as he was halfway up, the man stepped on the back of his hand and ground it, and someone below sucked in a breath. Ma Xiaobao clapped: "Good! Nice stomp! That's what you get for being Shen Xiaoman's friend!"

Xiaoman stood below and said nothing. His hands were clenched in his sleeves till the nails bit his palms. The ring of light behind his five doors, kicked by that stomp, surged up into his throat, so hot his eyes stung. He had only to take one step onto the stage — one step, and that man would turn three times in the air. But take that step, and the whole temple would see: a boy checked at layer two, written layer two in the register, stepping up and knocking a layer-three senior flying with one palm. The token on his chest was cool, and a very sleepy voice said just one word: "Hide."

He didn't step. The seventh time, Sun Ergou pushed himself up by his knees, face all blood, one string of the blue pouch snapped so it dangled at his hip. He caught it, tucked it back in his belt, and went at the man again — not charging, walking, one step at a time, legs shaking like a sieve, every step planted firm. The half stick burned out, and the steward struck the gong: "Stop. Sun Ergou, can you go on?" Sun Ergou spat a mouthful of bloody froth: "…I can." "I say you can't." Sun Ergou thought, and nodded: "…Then I can't." He bowed to the steward, bowed to the man too, and walked down off the stage by himself.

He let no one help him, walked all the way to the few steps at the edge of the ground and sat down hard, and once down he couldn't get up again. Xiaoman went over, stood before him a moment, and held out his hand: "Up. The ground's cold." Sun Ergou took it and Xiaoman pulled him up. Sun Ergou was half a head taller and nothing but bones; pulled up, he weighed nothing, like pulling up a bamboo pole. On the ninth of the ninth month, at the hundred-and-fortieth step, a boy from Yan had sat unable to get up, and Xiaoman had walked past without stopping. He'd thought then: when I stand steady enough, I'll pull. Today he wasn't standing all that steady either, but at least he'd pulled one.

That morning three rounds were fought on the platform, and thirty-two were whittled to four. Qi Changsong, first on the inner register, layer eight, twenty years standing post in the inner court, went up three times and never moved a step — he planted himself on the seam at the centre, feet as if nailed into the stone; opponents hit him and he didn't budge, pushed him and he didn't budge, and when the half stick burned out the steward looked, and the one at the centre was him. In the inner court they called him Immovable Qi. Qin Yan went up three times and never drew her sword; she tapped and nudged with the scabbard and three opponents walked off the stage by themselves. Ma Xiaobao's first two, the mirror left hanging at his waist, were one punch each, and his fists left two white marks in the bluestone. The strength of two layers in one night was real.

Third round: Ma Xiaobao against Lu the Loach. Before going up, Lu squeezed past Xiaoman and said low: "That mirror came up from Xiapi on my father's boat — Master Ma San hired my father's boat — and it sat in his hold all the way. Under the red cloth, one night, it lit up by itself — cold, like the light at the bottom of the Si. My father says it isn't for showing demons, it's for recognising things." Then he rubbed his hands and went up. Lu was a fisherman's son, slippery as his name, and his first punch ducked in under Ma Xiaobao's arm. Only then did Ma Xiaobao take off the mirror.

Below the stage Xiaoman saw it clearly: the mirror didn't light just by being raised. Ma Xiaobao held it in both hands, and the blotches on his face flared red and swelled patch by patch, as if something were being drawn out of him and poured into the mirror — only then did its face light, and a beam of yellow light hit Lu in the face. Lu yelped and staggered back clutching his eyes: "Cold! That light's cold — it goes for your heart!" He backed a step; Ma Xiaobao lit it again, the blotches flared again, and his shoulders heaved; at the third flash Lu missed his footing and fell off the stage. Ma Xiaobao stood holding the mirror, panting a long while before he got his breath. He jerked his chin at Xiaoman below.

The midday break. Zhou Heng stood on the platform, opened the blue register, cleared his throat and read: "Contest rules, article seventeen: an outer-court disciple who loses the first round may pay ten spirit stones for a second trial. The challenger takes on the one standing first on this year's outer register; if he wins, he takes that one's lot and the one challenged is out; if he loses, he is sent down, stones not refunded." When he'd read it he took a stick of incense from his coat, stuck it in the burner at the corner of the stage and lit it. "The break is one stick. Whoever wants a second trial, stones to the stewards' office before it burns out." And he added: "This article was set thirty years ago. Nobody's ever used it."

A moment's silence below, then a hum, and every head turned to Xiaoman. Ma Xiaobao's voice rose out of the crowd: "Him? Pay with what? He can't even scrape up one stone!" A burst of laughter. Xiaoman stood there, his face burning. He hadn't a single stone on him; whatever he'd had had gone to the common fund and the rice-bucket.

He went to the stewards' office anyway. Zhou Heng sat behind the table; on it burned half a candle — he only ever burned half, the other half broken off and kept in the drawer. "Brother Zhou, I want the second trial." "Ten." "I haven't got it. That 'to be settled' in the night-watch book… could it be settled now?" Zhou Heng glanced at him and went back to his ledger: "Laba accounts close in the evening. The outer court doesn't pay in advance. Rules are rules."

Xiaoman stood a moment and went out. Ma Xiaobao was leaning by the door, weighing a spirit stone in his palm — a bounce, a look at Xiaoman, another bounce; seeing him come out he threw it at his heels: "Pick it up. One. Nine to go." The followers roared. The stone rolled twice in the mud and stopped at the toe of Xiaoman's sandal. He looked at it and stepped over it. Behind him Ma Xiaobao said: "Shen Xiaoman, this year's pill is named Ma." The incense on the corner of the stage had burned halfway. On the steps Sun Ergou, a plaster from the kitchen auntie stuck crooked on his chin, grinned at him with blood still in his mouth. Under the pagoda tree Money-Keeper Qian was crossing out the "one to a hundred" after Shen Xiaoman with his charcoal, meaning to raise it; he thought, and put the charcoal down — a boy who'd lost the first round and couldn't pay ten stones had no odds worth writing; whatever you wrote, it came to nothing.

A He had got to the pagoda tree before him. She slapped the little folded slip down on the scale pan: "Shopkeeper, the one cash I bet — give it back." Qian raised his eyelids: "A bet is a bet. What's on the board is what I said — once it's bet, it's not returned." "I need it urgently." "Urgent or not, no. Give it back to you today and tomorrow everyone comes for theirs, and this board of mine isn't clean any more." A He bit her lip, stood a while, and said no more.

A He turned and saw Xiaoman. She said nothing, put the slip back in her notebook and walked past him. Xiaoman knew what she'd wanted the cash for: one cash, and ten spirit stones a world away from it; but one cash was all she had.

Under the pagoda tree Xiaoman stopped. In his sleeve was a little porcelain bottle — the chilli-oil bottle the kitchen threw out, which he had washed seven times at the well himself — and in it one pill, the healing pill that had rolled out from under the rice-bucket's heap of junk in the tenth month, nine gold lines. It was for his father's knees — through the half month in the tenth month when he walked the night watch on a broken rib, he hadn't been able to bring himself to eat it. On Money-Keeper Qian's scale it would fetch not ten stones but a hundred. But no one in the outer court had ever seen a pill with nine gold lines; bring it out, and the first question would be where from — and he couldn't answer that; and if he couldn't, they would search him, search the woodshed, and the rice-bucket couldn't stay hidden, and nor could Yinyue. And it was his father's. He gripped the bottle a long time, till it was warm in his hand, and in the end didn't take it out.

label.en: Pawn grandfather's bow; take the second trial

story.zh:
他转身往大通铺跑。门口那张铺，褥子底下压着一张弓。

弓背上十七道牛筋，缠得紧紧的，是爷爷缠的，他爹重缠过的。九月初四夜里，他爹一瘸一拐地把它从墙上摘下来，塞进他怀里：「你爷爷的。」去年秋天，马三站在他家门口，说这张弓眼看便要姓马；他家拼了一冬，才把它留在了沈家的墙上。

小满把弓抽出来，在手里握了一握。弓背是凉的，握久了，便温了。他没有再想，背上它，跑回了老槐树底下。

「掌柜的。你收当么？」

钱掌柜抬起眼皮，看见那张弓，算盘珠子停了。他伸手接过来，掂了一掂，拿指甲弹了弹弓背，侧着耳朵听；又把弓背凑到眼前，顺着木纹看了好一会儿，看得很慢，跟方才看那一文钱、看马小宝那一袋灵石，都不是一个看法。看完了，他把弓横放在秤盘上，秤杆却没动，道：「牛筋十七道，值三钱银子。弦是新的，值五十文。这木头——」他顿了一顿，「我叫不出名字。你要几块？」

小满道：「十块。」钱掌柜道：「叫不出名字的东西，我当它一回押宝。十块。当期到今夜子时。子时以前，十块灵石拿来，弓还你，另收三十文利钱，一文不多，半文不少；子时一过，弓便姓钱了。」他从秤杆上那只小布袋里一块一块往外数灵石，数一块，在当票上画一道，「这当票，你自己收好。」

小满接过当票，接过那十块灵石，没有回头看那张弓。他走出几步，听见钱掌柜在他身后道：「沈小满。」他站住了。钱掌柜拨着算盘，眼睛也不抬：「这张弓，我替你挂在板子背面。不给人看。」

台角那炷香，还剩一指。小满把十块灵石拍在执事房的桌上。周衡看了一眼灵石，又看了一眼他背上——空了——拿笔在账上记了一行，一个字也没有问。

复试，挑外门名册上排头一个。排头一个，是秦雁。周衡把第十七条又念了一遍，念到「被挑者出局」，台下一片哗然：她上午三场都赢了，进了四强；这一场要是输了，三年的队便白排了；赢了，也不过是回到原地。周衡看着她：「秦雁，你接不接？」规矩上她不能不接，周衡却还是问了。秦雁道：「接。」

台角的水缸边上，两个人碰上了。秦雁舀了半瓢水，没喝，递给了他。小满接过来喝了，道：「秦师姐。秘境里那一回……」秦雁道：「你没往下坠。我记得。」她又舀了一瓢，自己喝了，望着台上那炷香，「你知道我为什么排了三年？」小满摇头。秦雁道：「进了内门，一月十块灵石，能折银子寄家。我爹前年叫熊把腿咬了，躺到如今。今年是我排头。」她把瓢放回缸沿上，「你这一场赢了，我明年再排；你这一场输了，十块灵石是周衡的。」她看着他，「我不让你。你也别让我。」

小满捧着那瓢，半天没说出话来。他想说「我不上了」，话到嘴边，想起钱掌柜板子背面挂着的那张弓，想起孙二狗石阶上那一口血，又咽了回去。他把瓢放下。秦雁点了点头，先上了台。
story.en:
He turned and ran for the long bunk. Under the mat of the bunk by the door lay a bow.

Seventeen wraps of ox sinew round its back, wound tight — his grandfather's wrapping, his father's rewrapping. On the night of the fourth of the ninth month his father had limped to the wall, taken it down and pushed it into his arms: "Your grandfather's." Last autumn Ma San had stood at their door and said that bow was about to become the Mas'; his family had fought a whole winter to keep it on the Shen family's wall.

Xiaoman drew the bow out and held it a moment. Its back was cold; held a while, it grew warm. He didn't think any further. He slung it on and ran back to the pagoda tree.

"Shopkeeper. Do you take pawns?" Money-Keeper Qian raised his eyelids, saw the bow, and his abacus beads stopped. He took it, hefted it, flicked its back with a fingernail and listened with his head on one side; then held the back up to his eye and followed the grain a long while, very slowly — not the way he had looked at that one cash, nor at Ma Xiaobao's bag of stones. When he was done he laid the bow across the scale pan, but the beam didn't move. "Seventeen wraps of sinew, worth three mace of silver. The string's new, worth fifty cash. This wood —" he paused, "I can't put a name to it. A thing I can't name, I don't price high and I don't beat down. Ten stones."

Qian raised his eyelids, saw the bow, and the abacus beads stopped. He took it, weighed it, flicked the stave with a fingernail and cocked his ear; then held the stave close and followed the grain a good while, slowly — not the way he'd looked at the one cash, nor at Ma Xiaobao's bag of stones. When he had looked he laid the bow across the pan, but the steelyard didn't move. "Seventeen wraps of ox sinew: three qian of silver. The string's new: fifty cash. This wood —" he paused. "I can't name it. How many do you want?"

"Ten," said Xiaoman. "A thing I can't put a name to," said Qian, "I'll take as a wager once. Ten. The pawn runs till midnight tonight. Bring ten stones before midnight and the bow's yours again, plus thirty cash interest — not one cash more, not half a cash less. Past midnight, the bow's a Qian." He counted the stones out of the little bag on his steelyard one by one, drawing a line on the pawn ticket for each. "Keep this ticket yourself."

Xiaoman took the ticket and the ten stones and didn't look back at the bow. A few steps on he heard Qian behind him: "Shen Xiaoman." He stopped. Qian worked his abacus without looking up: "I'll hang the bow on the back of the board for you. Nobody sees it."

The incense at the stage's corner had a finger's width left. Xiaoman slapped the ten stones on the table in the stewards' office. Zhou Heng looked at the stones, then at his back — empty now — wrote a line in his ledger, and asked not one word.

The second trial: take on the one standing first on the outer register. First on the outer register was Qin Yan. Zhou Heng read article seventeen again, and at "the one challenged is out" the crowd erupted: she had won all three bouts that morning and was in the last four; lose this one and her three years of queuing were for nothing; win it, and she was only back where she'd been. Zhou Heng looked at her: "Qin Yan, do you accept?" By the rules she couldn't refuse, and still Zhou Heng asked. "I accept," said Qin Yan.

By the water vat at the corner of the stage the two of them met. Qin Yan ladled half a scoop and didn't drink it; she handed it to him. Xiaoman drank. "Sister Qin. That time in the hidden realm…" "You didn't hang. I remember." She ladled another and drank it herself, watching the incense on the stage. "Do you know why I've queued three years?" Xiaoman shook his head. "In the inner court it's ten stones a month, and you can change them into silver and send it home. Two years ago a bear took my father's leg; he's been lying down ever since. This year I'm first in line." She set the ladle on the vat's rim. "If you win this bout, I queue again next year; if you lose, the ten stones are Zhou Heng's." She looked at him. "I won't give way to you. Don't you give way to me."

Xiaoman held the ladle and couldn't say a word for a long time. He wanted to say, "I won't go up"; it got as far as his lips, and then he thought of the bow hanging on the back of Qian's board, and of the mouthful of blood on the steps from Sun Ergou, and swallowed it. He set the ladle down. Qin Yan nodded and went up onto the stage first.
